With no project drawing, part number or customer approval behind them, the page publishes no production, stock or case-study claim. project-inputs Project inputs Three inputs can start the engineering review A drawing, a 3D model and a physical sample all enter the same assessment route. Each one asks something different of you, so each card states what the review needs before it can begin. 2D drawing Dimensions, datums and tolerance intent Provide dimensions, datums, critical characteristics, tolerance intent, material or performance requirements and the applicable revision. For a vehicle without a spare wheel, the interruption can be even more immediate. Self-sealing technology is intended to reduce the immediate interruption caused by an applicable tread puncture. It does not prevent every form of tyre damage. 01 Air loss after a tread puncture A penetrating object can create an air-loss path and force the driver to respond before continuing the journey. 02 Changing a tyre at the roadside The driver may not have the tools, experience or safe working space required for a roadside wheel change. 03 Repair or replacement Workshop time and the condition of the tyre determine whether inspection, repair or replacement is required. 04 Towing and delay Waiting for roadside assistance adds cost and interrupts personal, commercial or fleet travel. T02 SELF-SEALING TYRE TECHNOLOGY A sealing layer responds around an applicable tread puncture A polymer-composite sealing layer is applied to the tyre inner liner. When an object penetrates the tread, the material surrounds it and helps limit air loss. After the object is removed, the material closes the puncture channel. Normal road use The product concept is intended to help limit immediate air loss from an applicable puncture through the tread area. The puncture area matters The illustrated response concerns the tread and internal sealing layer. Sidewall, shoulder, impact and structural damage require a different assessment. Self-sealing describes the behaviour of the internal sealing layer. It does not mean that the tyre is immune to damage or that professional inspection is unnecessary. See how the sealing layer responds T03 HOW IT RESPONDS The material closes around the puncture channel 01 Object enters the tread area The object passes through the tread and into the sealing layer on the inner liner. 02 The material surrounds the object The sealing material closes around the penetrating object and helps limit the air path while it remains in place. 03 The channel closes after removal When the object is removed, the material recovers over the channel. The tyre still requires inspection to confirm its condition. This sequence illustrates the stated sealing mechanism in the tested tread area. pages.text_excerpt: Insights 06 dossiers Guides for Dealers and Wheel Shops Fitment, construction, finishing and importing — the technical groundwork that decides whether a forged wheel order goes smoothly. Written for the person quoting the job, not the person reading a brochure. Six working guides. Each opens as a full article, or expands in place for the short version. Browse the guides Ask a technical question Fitment and manufacturing decisions begin with a reviewable specification. Technical library How to use these Read the part that matches the problem in front of you These are working notes rather than marketing pages. They cover the six questions that come up most often between a dealer and a factory — and each one is the kind of question that is cheap to answer before an order and expensive to answer after. All guides Logistics Finishing Fitment Construction 6 reference guides Commercial and shipping terms are confirmed for each destination market. 01 Logistics 7 min read Importing wheels: freight and duties Incoterms, HS codes, duty and the paperwork trail — a dealer's checklist for getting wheels across a border without a customs hold. Read guide Quick preview Expand for the short version, or open the full guide for the working detail. Agree the incoterm before you price the job FOB, CIF and DDP are not interchangeable labels — they move who is responsible for freight, insurance, duty and clearance, and therefore move the landed cost materially. Quoting a customer before the incoterm is agreed is how margin disappears. PLACEHOLDER: confirm which incoterms Fenghuai actually offers and which it will not, and produce a one-page explanation for dealers. Classification and duty Wheels need a correct HS classification and a stated country of origin on the commercial invoice. Get the description wrong and the consignment stops at the border while it is resolved — usually at the worst possible moment for the customer. Duty and tax rates vary by destination and by classification. They must be calculated for the destination market rather than assumed from a previous shipment. Packing and damage claims Wheels are heavy and awkward, and once they are on a pallet they are handled by machinery rather than people. Freight-grade packing with reinforced corners is cheaper than a damage claim that takes eight weeks to resolve. Photograph the consignment before it leaves and on arrival, and keep the inspection record with the shipment documentation — it is what a claim is decided on. Finish availability is confirmed for the selected model and order. 02 Finishing 5 min read Finishing options explained Brushed, polished, satin, matte and gloss — what each finish is, how it ages, and how to avoid a colour mismatch between samples and a delivered order. Read guide Quick preview Expand for the short version, or open the full guide for the working detail. Surface versus colour Finishes have two independent attributes that customers often conflate. Surface texture — brushed, polished, satin, matte, gloss — describes how the metal interacts with light. Colour describes its hue. You can have a matte bronze and a gloss bronze; they are the same colour with different surface behaviour. Getting this distinction clear early prevents most finish disputes. Why swatches lie A flat colour swatch cannot show how linear grain catches light as a wheel turns, how a gloss behaves in direct sunlight, or how a finish reads against a specific body colour. Screen calibration changes it again. For anything other than a straightforward gloss or matte black, ask for a physical sample or a photograph of the exact finish on an actual wheel before committing a full order. Repeatability The real risk with finishes is not the first order — it is the second one. Repeatability depends on controlled process stages and on keeping a record of what was actually supplied. Ask what finish the previous order was, not what it was called. Approved wheel media; specifications remain model and variant specific. 03 Fitment 6 min read How to measure your fitment The five numbers a forged wheel order actually needs, how to read them off a vehicle, and why a tape measure alone will get you into trouble. Read guide Quick preview Expand for the short version, or open the full guide for the working detail. The five numbers that matter A forged wheel order is specified by five values: diameter, width, offset, PCD (bolt pattern) and centre bore. Everything else — face profile, lip depth, spoke concavity — follows from how those five interact with the vehicle. Diameter and width are straightforward and are the numbers customers quote. Offset is where most orders go wrong, because it is invisible to anyone who has not measured it and it changes how the wheel sits relative to the arch, the suspension and the brake caliper. Measuring offset without a wheel off the car Offset (ET) is the distance from the wheel's mounting face to its centreline, in millimetres. Positive means the mounting face is outboard of the centreline; negative means inboard. The reliable route for a vehicle that is new to you is to start from the OEM specification for that exact trim, then adjust deliberately and in small steps. If you are measuring a physical wheel, backspacing (the distance from the mounting face to the inboard edge) is easier to measure directly and converts back to offset once you know the width. What to send the factory Photograph the vehicle with the arch visible, note any brake or suspension modification, and give us the OEM specification you are starting from along with the stance you are targeting. We will check clearance and load rating against it and flag anything that will not fit before material is cut. Geometry should be checked from a recorded baseline, not appearance alone. 04 Fitment 5 min read Understanding offset and backspacing Two ways of describing the same measurement, and the conversion that stops a customer's wheel from sitting 15mm further out than they expected. Read guide Quick preview Expand for the short version, or open the full guide for the working detail. They describe the same thing from opposite ends Offset is measured from the wheel centreline. Backspacing is measured from the mounting face to the inboard lip. One is wheel-centric, the other is car-centric, and confusion between them is a common reason a quoted fitment comes out wrong. For a given width, the two are directly related — which means converting between them requires knowing the width, and a specification quoting backspacing without a width is incomplete. Why it matters at the arch On a wide-body or lowered car, the constraint is usually not the outboard arch but the inboard clearance: the inner lip against the suspension strut, control arm or brake caliper. pages.text_excerpt: / Insights / Bolt patterns Reference Bolt Pattern Guides A bolt pattern defines how a wheel mounts to the hub: how many fixing points, and the diameter of the circle they sit on. These guides explain what the two numbers mean, how to measure a pattern on a real wheel, and how to size a spigot — with the vehicle lists clearly marked as a starting point rather than a fitment authority. Three guides today: 5x112, 5x114.3 and 5x120. Each one leads with the method, not the list. Open a pattern guide Send your vehicle details Safety-critical fitment data Measure your own bolt pattern — do not trust a list Bolt pattern is the circle the wheel's mounting holes sit on, and getting it wrong is a wheel-loss risk, not a styling problem. The vehicle lists on these pages are starting points for research only: they are compiled from public references, not from Fenghuai engineering data, and they are not a fitment guarantee. Identify your pattern by measuring the wheel or the hub, or by checking your vehicle's factory documentation for the exact trim, brake package and model year. Fenghuai confirms PCD, centre bore and offset per order before anything is manufactured. Three guides Pick your pattern The vehicle references below are compiled from public sources and are NOT verified fitment data. Always confirm against your specific vehicle before ordering. 5x112 Verify against your specific vehicle Five-stud, 112 mm circle 5x112 is a five-stud pattern on a 112 mm bolt circle, used across a large share of European production cars. The pattern name is fixed; the centre bore and offset that go with it are not — they vary by platform, generation and brake package, which is why the pattern alone never defines a wheel. Read the guide 5x114.3 Verify against your specific vehicle Five-stud, 114.3 mm circle 5x114.3 is a five-stud pattern on a 114.3 mm bolt circle — the metric expression of the pattern many sources still publish in inches as 5x4.5. Because 114.3 mm and 4.5 inches describe the same circle, the two names are interchangeable; because sources mix them, the ambiguity is a common source of ordering errors. Read the guide 5x120 Verify against your specific vehicle Five-stud, 120 mm circle 5x120 is a five-stud pattern on a 120 mm bolt circle. It is most strongly associated with BMW and a number of other rear-drive European platforms, and it is a pattern where the vehicle lists are particularly misleading — several marques use both 5x120 and other patterns across their ranges, so a badge is never an answer. Read the guide The method How to identify the pattern you actually have Two reliable routes: read the marking on your existing wheel, or measure the pattern directly. Both are covered in each guide, and the measuring method is the same for every pattern. Ask us to confirm Offset calculator Count the fixing points first — that half is easy and unambiguous. For an odd count, measure centre-of-one to outer-edge-of-the-opposite. For an even count, measure centre-to-centre across the widest span. Read the marking on the wheel and check it matches your measurement. Confirm centre bore as well — the pattern alone does not centre a wheel. Questions Bolt pattern FAQ Is 5x114 the same as 5x114.3? Not necessarily, and you should not assume it. 5x114.3 is the pattern, and 114.3 mm is exactly 4.5 inches — which is why the same pattern is published as 5x4.5 in inch-unit sources. A listing written 5x114 may be correct metric notation inexpertly rounded, or a transcription error. Convert, measure, and confirm before treating them as the same. Can I use an adapter to change my bolt pattern? Wheel adapters exist and are used in the aftermarket, but they change the offset and add a fastened interface between the hub and the wheel. On a custom order there is no reason to accept that: we manufacture the wheel with your pattern and centre bore, which removes the adapter and the risk it carries. We do not recommend adapters as a substitute for a correctly specified forged wheel. How do I measure a five-stud pattern correctly? You cannot measure straight across, because no fixing sits directly opposite another. Measure from the centre of one fixing point to the outer edge of the roughly opposite fixing point — that span equals the bolt circle diameter. Measuring centre-to-centre between two adjacent fixings gives a smaller, plausible-looking number that identifies nothing. Where is the pattern marked on a wheel? Usually cast, stamped or moulded on the inside face of the wheel or under the centre cap, often next to the offset and sometimes the centre bore. Look for a group like 5x114.3. Where it is illegible, your vehicle's factory documentation for the exact trim is a better reference than any published pattern list. Does the bolt pattern alone tell me a wheel will fit? No. A wheel needs the correct pattern to bolt on, but it also needs the correct centre bore to centre on the hub, an offset that clears the suspension, brakes and arch, and a load rating suited to the vehicle. We confirm all of those together per order. Can you look up my car's bolt pattern for me? We will confirm the specification for your vehicle when you order, but we deliberately do not publish per-vehicle pattern data as verified fact, because a figure that is right for one trim, generation or brake package can be wrong for the next. The reliable answers come from measuring your own vehicle or from its factory documentation. pages.text_excerpt: / Tools / Offset calculator Tool Wheel Offset Calculator Compare a wheel you have against a wheel you are considering, and see exactly how much further the new one reaches — inward toward the suspension, and outward toward the arch. Enter both wheels below. The result is a planning figure: it models width, offset and diameter, and nothing else. Use the calculator Send your vehicle details The basics What wheel offset actually is Offset — written as ET on the wheel, from the German Einpresstiefe — is the distance in millimetres from the wheel's mounting face to its centreline. It describes where the wheel sits on the hub, not how wide it is. Positive offset means the mounting face sits outboard of the centreline: the wheel tucks further under the arch, with more of its width inboard. Negative offset means the mounting face sits inboard of the centreline: the wheel sits further out, with more of its width outboard. Zero offset puts the mounting face exactly on the centreline. The consequence people miss is that offset and width interact. Fitting a wider wheel at the same offset moves both edges outward — and the inboard edge is the one that fouls the strut, the control arm or the brake caliper. That is why this calculator reports the inboard change as well as the outer poke. The tool Compare two wheels Planning aid — not a fitment approval Check the result against the real car before you order This calculator models wheel width, offset and diameter only. It does not account for brake caliper shape, suspension travel, camber, arch or liner clearance, or the load rating your vehicle requires. It cannot tell you whether a wheel will physically fit. Fenghuai confirms the final specification against your specific vehicle before an order is cut, and any figure below is a starting point for that conversation rather than a substitute for it. Start from an illustrative preset Wider, same offset 8.0J ET35 → 9.0J ET35, 18" both Same width, lower offset 9.0J ET45 → 9.0J ET30, 19" both Plus-size, wider 8.5J ET40 19" → 9.5J ET35 20" Deep-dish conversion 10.0J ET40 → 11.0J ET15, 20" both Reset Presets are made-up round numbers used to demonstrate the arithmetic. They are not any vehicle's actual factory specification. Outer edge moves 12.7 mm further out — more poke, and that much less arch clearance. Working, in millimetres Original backspace 136.6 mm Replacement backspace 149.3 mm Original frontspace 66.6 mm Replacement frontspace 79.3 mm Planning aid only. Brake caliper shape, suspension travel, camber, arch clearance and load rating are confirmed by Fenghuai against your vehicle before an order is cut. The formula How the numbers are worked out The calculator works from backspace — the distance from the mounting face to the wheel's inner edge — which is the value that determines inboard clearance. backspace(mm) = (width_in × 25.4) / 2 + offset_mm frontspace(mm) = (width_in × 25.4) / 2 − offset_mm innerChange(mm) = newBackspace − oldBackspace outerChange(mm) = newFrontspace − oldFrontspace diameterChange(in) = newDiameter − oldDiameter A positive innerChange means the inner edge moves further into the car, reducing inboard clearance. A positive outerChange means the outer edge moves further out, increasing poke. Both edges also move outward by half the diameter change, because a larger wheel reaches further in every direction from the hub. Reading the result What the output tells you, and what it does not Inner clearance change How much closer the wheel's inner edge sits to the suspension, relative to the original. A positive figure means less room than before — the single most common cause of a fitment that rubs. Outer poke / clearance change How much further the wheel's outer edge sits from the hub, relative to the original. A positive figure means more poke. On a car with limited arch room, that is where rubbing on the arch or liner appears. Diameter change A larger diameter reaches further both inboard and outboard by half the increase, regardless of offset. It also changes rolling radius, which affects speedometer accuracy and gearing. What it cannot see Brake caliper shape and spoke clearance, suspension travel under compression, camber change, arch liner and brake ducting. A result inside the original envelope is a good sign, not an approval. Worked examples Two illustrative examples ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY. These examples use made-up round numbers to show how the arithmetic behaves — they are not any vehicle's actual stock specification, and must not be used as a lookup. Confirm the real values for your vehicle before relying on them. Wider wheel, same offset 8.0J ET35 → 9.0J ET35, same diameter The width is 25.4 mm greater, so each edge moves outward by 12.7 mm. Inboard clearance drops by 12.7 mm and poke rises by 12.7 mm. This is the change that catches people out: they only budgeted for the extra poke. Same width, lower offset 9.0J ET45 → 9.0J ET30, same diameter The width is unchanged, so the whole wheel shifts outboard by the 15 mm offset change. Poke rises by 15 mm and inboard clearance improves by 15 mm. This is the cheap way to gain brake clearance — with the trade-off that the outer edge moves out. Offset types Positive, zero and negative offset Every production car is built around a particular offset range. Moving far outside it changes steering geometry, wheel bearing load and how the car behaves under braking, whether or not the wheel physically fits. Most common on modern cars Positive offset The mounting face is outboard of the centreline, so most of the wheel's width sits inboard. Modern front-wheel-drive and most all-wheel-drive cars use relatively high positive offsets because it keeps the scrub radius small and the steering axis inside the tyre contact patch. Common on older rear-drive cars Zero offset The mounting face sits on the centreline, splitting the width evenly either side. It is characteristic of older rear-drive platforms and of wheels designed for a deep-lip look where the lip is a genuine part of the geometry rather than styling. Deep-dish and off-road Negative offset The mounting face is inboard of the centreline, pushing the wheel outboard. It produces the deep-dish appearance and is common on lifted trucks and off-road builds. On a road car it increases the load on the hub and wheel bearings and changes steering feel, so it should be a deliberate decision, not an accident of the wheel you bought. Questions Offset calculator FAQ Can I fit a wider wheel at the same offset? Sometimes, but the constraint is usually the inboard edge rather than the arch. Adding width at the same offset moves both edges outward equally, so inboard clearance falls by half the width increase in millimetres. Run the numbers above and check whether the original wheel had that much room to give — on a car with a large brake package it often did not. Does a lower offset always mean more poke? For the same width and diameter, yes: lowering the offset moves the whole wheel outboard, so the outer edge moves out and the inboard edge moves away from the suspension. It is the standard way to gain brake clearance, at the cost of arch clearance and a change in steering geometry. Why does the calculator ask for diameter?
